notes: “¿Cómo estás?” uses tú, for friends and family. With strangers, older people or at work, use usted and drop the -s: “¿Cómo está?”.
“Quisiera” (I would like) sounds softer than “quiero” (I want). It is the usual way to order in a café.

type: grammar tip: “Estar” for where things are
notes: Use estar, not ser, to say where something is: “¿Dónde está…?” and “Está aquí”.

type: grammar tip: Present tense of -ar verbs
notes: Drop -ar and add the ending: trabajar → trabajo (I work), trabajas (you work), trabaja (he/she works).

type: grammar tip: Nouns have a gender
notes: Every noun is masculine or feminine, and the article and adjective match it: el hermano alto, la hermana alta.
Use cuesta for one thing and cuestan for more than one.
Spanish says the weather “makes” heat: hace calor, hace frío, hace sol. For rain, say “llueve”.
“Me gusta” means “it pleases me”. Use gusta with a verb or one thing, and gustan with several things.

type: grammar tip: “Hay”: there is, there are
text (target language): Hay una mesa en la cocina
english meaning: There is a table in the kitchen
notes: Hay works for one thing or many: hay una cama (there is a bed), hay dos ventanas (there are two windows).
Spanish says the body part hurts you: me duele la cabeza (my head hurts). Use duelen for more than one: me duelen los pies.
Routine verbs often take me, te, se: levantarse → me levanto (I get up), acostarse → me acuesto (I go to bed).
Feelings use estar, because they change: está cansado (he is tired), estoy triste (I am sad).
“Comment ça va ?” is casual. With strangers, at work or with older people, say “Comment allez-vous ?”.
“Je voudrais” (I would like) comes from vouloir. It is more polite than “je veux”.

english meaning: The station is on the left
notes: Use “à” for directions: à gauche (on the left), à droite (on the right), tout droit (straight on).

type: grammar tip: Present tense of -er verbs
notes: travailler → je travaille, tu travailles, il travaille. These three forms all sound the same.
“My” matches the noun: mon frère (masculine), ma mère (feminine), mes parents (plural).
“Combien ça coûte ?” and “C’est combien ?” both mean “How much is it?”. The second is very common in shops.
Most weather uses il fait: il fait chaud, il fait froid, il fait beau. Rain is different: il pleut.
Put the verb straight after aimer: j’aime lire, j’aime nager. For “I don’t like”, wrap it in ne… pas.

type: grammar tip: “Il y a”: there is
text (target language): Il y a une table dans la cuisine
english meaning: There is a table in the kitchen
notes: Il y a works for one thing or many: il y a un lit, il y a deux fenêtres.
To say something hurts, use avoir mal à + body part: j’ai mal à la tête (head), j’ai mal au dos (back).
Routine verbs take me, te, se: se lever → je me lève (I get up), se coucher → je me couche (I go to bed).

type: grammar tip: Adjectives match the person
notes: Adjectives change for a woman, often by adding -e: fatigué → fatiguée. Some change more: heureux → heureuse.

type: grammar tip: です makes it polite
notes: Ending a sentence with です (desu) makes it polite. わたしは アレックスです means “As for me, I’m Alex”.
Say the thing, then を ください (o kudasai) to ask for it politely.

type: grammar tip: は and どこ
text (target language): トイレは どこですか？
notes: X は どこですか？ means “Where is X?”. は marks the topic; it is written “ha” but said “wa”.

type: grammar tip: で: where you do something
text (target language): うちで はたらきます
notes: で (de) marks the place where an action happens: オフィスで はたらきます (I work at the office).

text (target language): おかあさんは げんきですか？
notes: Talking about your own family uses humble words (はは, my mother). For someone else’s family, use polite words (おかあさん).

type: grammar tip: これ, それ, あれ
text (target language): それは いくらですか？
notes: これ is this (near me), それ is that (near you), あれ is that over there.

text (target language): きのうは さむかったです
notes: Adjectives like あつい, さむい and たかい end in い and can finish a sentence with です. For the past, change い to かった.

type: grammar tip: が すきです: I like
text (target language): おんがくが すきです
notes: X が すきです means “I like X”. The thing you like comes first.

type: grammar tip: あります and います
text (target language): へやに ねこが います
english meaning: There is a cat in the room
notes: Use あります for things and います for people and animals: いすが あります (there is a chair), ねこが います (there is a cat).

type: grammar tip: いたい: it hurts
notes: Body part + が + いたいです says something hurts: あたまが いたいです (I have a headache).

text (target language): わたしは じゅうじに ねます
english meaning: I go to bed at ten
notes: Put に after a clock time: しちじに (at seven). Verbs ending in ます are polite and cover both now and later.

type: grammar tip: Feelings with です
text (target language): とても かなしいです
notes: Add です to an い-adjective to sound polite: うれしい → うれしいです (I am happy).
“Wie geht es dir?” is informal. With strangers and at work, use Sie: “Wie geht es Ihnen?”.
This is the polite way to order. “Einen Kaffee” uses einen because Kaffee is masculine and the object of the sentence.
Every noun has a gender: der Bahnhof, die Fahrkarte, das Hotel. Learn the article together with the word.

type: grammar tip: The verb comes second
notes: In a statement the verb is always the second idea. If you start with another word, the subject moves after the verb.
“My” matches the noun: mein Bruder (masculine), meine Mutter (feminine).

english meaning: I would like to buy that
notes: Möchte (would like) sends the second verb to the end of the sentence: Ich möchte bezahlen.

type: grammar tip: Talking about the weather
notes: Use es: Es ist kalt, es ist heiß. Rain is a verb: Es regnet.
Add gern after the verb to say you like doing it: Ich lese gern. Not liking it: nicht gern.

text (target language): Es gibt einen Stuhl in der Küche
english meaning: There is a chair in the kitchen
notes: Es gibt works for one thing or many: es gibt einen Tisch, es gibt zwei Fenster.
German joins words into one: Kopf (head) + Schmerzen (pain) = Kopfschmerzen. Bauch (stomach) → Bauchschmerzen.
Some verbs split in two: aufstehen → ich stehe um sieben auf. The prefix goes to the end.
To say how you are, use mir geht es + a word: mir geht es gut (I’m fine), mir geht es schlecht (I’m not well).
Ending with -요 (yo) is polite but friendly, right for most conversations: 지내요, 고마워요.

type: grammar tip: 주세요: please give me
notes: Say the thing, then 주세요 (juseyo), to ask for it.
Use 이 after a consonant (역이) and 가 after a vowel (표가).

type: grammar tip: 에서: where you do something
notes: 에서 (eseo) marks the place where an action happens: 사무실에서 일해요 (I work at the office).
Use 은 after a consonant and 는 after a vowel: 저는 (as for me), 형은 (as for my brother).
얼마예요? means “How much is it?”. Put the item first: 사과 얼마예요?

type: grammar tip: Adjectives work like verbs
notes: Korean adjectives are full sentences on their own: 더워요 (it’s hot), 추워요 (it’s cold).
Thing + 을/를 + 좋아해요. Use 을 after a consonant and 를 after a vowel.

english meaning: There is a bed in the room

Body part + 이/가 + 아파요: 머리가 아파요 (my head hurts), 배가 아파요 (my stomach hurts).

english meaning: I go to bed at ten

Feeling words work like verbs: 행복해요 (I’m happy), 피곤해요 (I’m tired). Raise your voice at the end to ask.

type: grammar tip: 吗 makes a question
notes: Add 吗 (ma) to the end of a statement to turn it into a yes/no question.
Numbers need a measure word before the noun: 一杯咖啡 (a cup of coffee), 一个苹果 (an apple).

type: grammar tip: 在 for where things are
notes: X 在哪里？ means “Where is X?”. 在 (zài) means “is at”.

type: grammar tip: Place before the verb
notes: Say where you do something before the verb: 我在家工作 (I at home work).
我的 means “my”. With close family and friends you can leave out 的: 我妈妈.

type: grammar tip: 多少钱: how much
notes: 多少钱？ means “how much money?”. Put the item first: 这个多少钱？
Chinese links a subject to an adjective with 很 (hěn) instead of “is”: 今天很热.

type: grammar tip: 喜欢: to like
notes: 喜欢 (xǐhuan) can take a noun or a verb: 我喜欢书, 我喜欢看书.

english meaning: There is a table in the kitchen
notes: 有 (yǒu) means both “there is” and “to have”. 没有 (méiyǒu) is the negative.
Body part + 疼 (téng): 头疼 (headache), 牙疼 (toothache). No verb for “have” is needed.

type: grammar tip: Time comes before the verb
english meaning: I go to bed at ten
notes: Chinese puts the time before the action: 我七点起床 is literally “I seven o’clock get up”.
Adjectives need no word for “is”, but usually take 很 (hěn): 我很累 (I am tired).
“Come stai?” is informal. With strangers, use Lei and the verb form for he/she: “Come sta?”.
“Vorrei” (I would like) comes from volere. It is the usual way to order.
Dove + è shortens to dov’è (where is). For several things: dove sono?

type: grammar tip: Present tense of -are verbs
notes: lavorare → lavoro (I work), lavori (you work), lavora (he/she works).

type: grammar tip: No article with one relative
notes: With a single family member, “my” needs no article: mia madre. With plurals it does: le mie sorelle.
Use costa for one thing and costano for more than one.
Italian uses fare: fa caldo, fa freddo, fa bel tempo. Rain is a verb: piove.
Use piace with a verb or one thing, and piacciono with several things.

english meaning: There is a table in the kitchen
notes: C’è is “there is”, ci sono is “there are”: c’è un letto, ci sono due finestre.
Ho mal di + body part says something hurts: ho mal di testa, ho mal di denti (toothache).
Routine verbs take mi, ti, si: alzarsi → mi alzo (I get up), svegliarsi → mi sveglio (I wake up).

type: grammar tip: Adjectives match the person
notes: Adjectives ending in -o change to -a for a woman: stanco → stanca. Ones ending in -e stay the same: felice.
आप (aap) is respectful: use it with strangers and elders. तुम (tum) is for friends.

type: grammar tip: मुझे … चाहिए: I want
notes: मुझे … चाहिए literally means “to me … is needed”. It is the everyday way to ask for something.

type: grammar tip: The verb comes last
notes: Hindi puts the verb at the end: होटल कहाँ है? is “Hotel where is?”.

text (target language): वह घर से काम करती है
notes: Many verbs change with the speaker’s or subject’s gender: करता हूँ (male), करती हूँ (female).
“My” matches what you own: मेरा भाई (my brother), मेरी माँ (my mother), मेरे दोस्त (my friends).
यह कितने का है? means “How much is this?”. For a feminine noun, use की: यह किताब कितने की है?

type: grammar tip: कल: yesterday or tomorrow
notes: कल (kal) means both. The verb’s tense tells you which one.

type: grammar tip: पसंद है: I like
notes: मुझे … पसंद है literally means “to me … is liked”.

english meaning: There is a table in the kitchen
notes: Use है for one thing and हैं for several: एक कुर्सी है, दो खिड़कियाँ हैं.

type: grammar tip: में दर्द है: it hurts
notes: Say मेरे + body part + में दर्द है: मेरे पेट में दर्द है (my stomach hurts).

type: grammar tip: Verbs follow the speaker
notes: A man says उठता हूँ, a woman says उठती हूँ. The -ता / -ती ending matches the person doing it.
Put क्या at the start to make a yes/no question: तुम ठीक हो → क्या तुम ठीक हो?

type: grammar tip: Present tense of -ar verbs
notes: trabalhar → trabalho (I work), trabalhas (you work), trabalha (he/she works).

Use custa for one thing and custam for more than one.

english meaning: There is a table in the kitchen
notes: Há works for one thing or many: há uma cama, há duas janelas. In Brazil people usually say “tem”.
Dói-me + one body part, doem-me + several: dói-me a cabeça, doem-me os pés.

english meaning: I go to bed at ten
notes: In Portugal the pronoun usually comes after the verb: levanto-me (I get up), deito-me (I go to bed).
Feelings use estar, because they change: está cansado (he is tired), estou triste (I am sad).
“Hoe gaat het?” works with anyone. To be formal, add “met u”: “Hoe gaat het met u?”.
Graag makes a request polite: “Ik wil graag…”. You can also ask “Mag ik…?” (May I have…?).
Nouns take de or het: de trein, het station. Learn the article with each word.

type: grammar tip: The verb comes second
notes: In a statement the verb is the second idea. Start with another word and the subject moves after the verb.
Dutch “my” is always mijn: mijn moeder, mijn broer, mijn ouders.
Use kost for one thing and kosten for more than one.

type: grammar tip: Talking about the weather
notes: Use het: Het is warm, het is koud. Rain is a verb: Het regent.
Put graag after the verb to say you like doing it: Ik lees graag. Not liking it: niet graag.

text (target language): Er is een tafel in de keuken

notes: Er is for one thing, er zijn for more: er is een bed, er zijn twee ramen.

работать → я работаю (I work), ты работаешь (you work), она работает (she works).

type: grammar tip: No “is” in the present
notes: Russian leaves out “is”: Мой брат высокий is literally “My brother tall”. Adjectives match gender: высокий, высокая.

notes: Weather often uses a single word: жарко (it’s hot), холодно (it’s cold). Rain “goes”: идёт дождь.

english meaning: I am glad to see you (woman speaking)

أريد (uriid) + the thing you want. Add من فضلك (min fadlak) to be polite.

أحب (uhibb) + a noun: أحب القراءة, “I love reading”.

english meaning: There is a chair in the kitchen

الساعة (as-saaʿa) + an ordinal number: الساعة السابعة (seven o’clock).

type: grammar tip: Feelings follow the speaker
notes: A man says سعيد (saʿiid), a woman says سعيدة (saʿiida). Most adjectives add ـة for a woman.
“Nasılsın?” is casual. To be polite, use the siz form: “Nasılsınız?”.
Put the thing first, then istiyorum. Bir means “a” or “one”.

type: grammar tip: The verb comes last

Verb + -mayı / -meyi + severim: okumayı severim, “I like reading”.

english meaning: There is a bed in the room

type: grammar tip: “I am” is an ending
notes: Add -(y)ım and friends to say “I am”: mutlu → mutluyum, yorgun → yorgunum.

type: grammar tip: Telling the time with “jam”

type: grammar tip: The verb comes second
english meaning: In the morning I drink coffee
notes: The verb is always the second part of a sentence: Klockan sju går jag upp (At seven I get up).
Adjectives add -t with ett-words and -a in the plural: glad, glatt, glada.

english meaning: How are you? (formal, to a woman)
notes: “Jak się masz?” is casual. To be polite, use Pan (to a man) or Pani (to a woman).
Poproszę + the thing is the easiest polite way to order or ask for something.
Gdzie jest + place asks where something is.
pracować → pracuję (I work), pracujesz (you work), pracuje (he/she works).
“My” matches the noun: mój brat, moja mama, moje dziecko (my child).
Use kosztuje for one thing and kosztują for several.

type: grammar tip: Talking about the weather
notes: Jest gorąco (it’s hot), jest zimno (it’s cold). Rain “falls”: pada deszcz.
Lubię (I like) + a verb in its basic form.

english meaning: There is a table in the kitchen
notes: Jest is “there is”, są is “there are”: w kuchni jest stół, są dwa okna.
Boli mnie + body part: boli mnie głowa (my head hurts). For several: bolą mnie nogi.
Many routine verbs take się: budzić się (to wake up) → budzę się o szóstej.

type: grammar tip: Adjectives follow the speaker
notes: A man says jestem zmęczony, a woman says jestem zmęczona.
